title: Resignation and notice period in India: what the law says in 2026
excerpt: How notice periods, garden leave, early release, relieving letters and full and final settlement work in India under the Labour Codes and 2026 standing orders.
content:
India has no single law that fixes how much notice a salaried office employee must give when resigning. Your notice period comes mainly from your appointment letter and HR policy, with a floor set by state shops and establishments laws and, for larger establishments, by standing orders under the Industrial Relations Code. Once you leave, the law is clearer: unpaid wages are due within two working days, and many workers are entitled to a service certificate within ten days.

Some of those rules are new. The four Labour Codes took effect on 21 November 2025, according to the Press Information Bureau, and on 8 May 2026 the Labour Ministry notified the Model Standing Orders, 2026, replacing the 1946 central rules on standing orders, according to Cyril Amarchand Mangaldas. In June 2026 the Bombay High Court also ruled on when an employer can hold back a relieving letter. This guide explains what applies to you, how garden leave and early release work, and what to expect in your full and final settlement. It is general information, not legal advice; for a dispute, confirm your position with a labour lawyer or your state labour department.

Key takeaways

  • For most private-sector office jobs, the notice period you must serve is whatever your contract says, within limits set by state law and fairness.
  • Standing orders apply only to establishments with 300 or more workers, and the Industrial Relations Code's "worker" excludes managers and supervisors earning above ₹18,000 a month.
  • Wages due to an employee who resigns must be paid within two working days of the resignation under the Code on Wages, 2019.
  • Garden leave is not defined in Indian law, but courts accept it during the notice period; post-exit non-competes are generally void.
  • A relieving letter is not a statutory right in every case. Courts have backed employers who withheld one after a breached service bond, and backed employees where a missing letter was used unfairly.

Where your notice period actually comes from

Three layers decide how much notice you owe. The first and usually decisive one is your employment contract and the company's HR policy. A law-firm practice note by Nishith Desai Associates, published through Thomson Reuters Practical Law and stating the law as at 1 November 2024, says contracts may set a longer period than any statutory minimum, but the arrangement must be reasonable, and labour courts look sceptically at a contract that lets the employer leave on one month's notice while holding the employee to three. The note cites the Supreme Court's 1986 judgment in Central Inland Water Transport Corporation v Brojo Nath Ganguly on unequal bargaining power (Nishith Desai Associates).

The second layer is state law. Shops and establishments Acts are state laws covering offices, shops and commercial establishments, and some set a notice period for employees who quit. The same practice note gives the Punjab Shops and Commercial Establishments Act, 1958 as an example: an employee with three months' continuous service must give 30 days' notice or pay in lieu. It adds that Maharashtra's law has no such notice clause, and that Delhi's 1954 Act sets one month's notice (or pay in lieu) on the employer's side for employees with at least three months' service. Where a state law sets the employee's notice, the note says a resigning employee may not need to serve a longer contractual period.

The third layer is standing orders, the certified service rules for larger industrial establishments. They matter less for white-collar staff than many people assume, for reasons explained below.

What changed under the Labour Codes

The government consolidated 29 central labour laws into four codes: the Code on Wages, 2019, the Industrial Relations Code, 2020, the Code on Social Security, 2020 and the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code, 2020, all in force from 21 November 2025 (PIB). The Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946, which older guides still cite, is among the laws folded into the Industrial Relations Code.

The central rules under all four codes were finalised on 8 and 9 May 2026, after draft rules published in December 2025 (Cyril Amarchand Mangaldas). The same alert notes that the central Model Standing Orders now apply across India, so states do not frame separate model orders, and employers covered by them need to review their own standing orders. State governments still have to finalise their own rules for establishments they regulate, which covers most private offices, so check your state's position.

Do standing orders cover you?

Probably not, if you are a manager or a well-paid engineer. Chapter IV of the Industrial Relations Code applies to industrial establishments with 300 or more workers on any day in the previous twelve months. The Code's definition of "worker" excludes people employed mainly in a managerial or administrative capacity, and supervisors earning more than ₹18,000 a month (Industrial Relations Code text, PRS Legislative Research).

If you are covered, the services-sector schedule of the Model Standing Orders, 2026 requires an employer ending a permanent worker's employment to give one month's notice or wages in lieu, and to pay wages and other dues before the end of the second working day after termination. It does not set a separate notice period for a worker who resigns (Model Standing Orders, 2026, S.O. 2312(E)).

Resigning: the practical sequence

  1. Read your appointment letter and HR policy first. Note the notice period, whether it differs during probation, whether buyout is allowed, whether leave can be adjusted, and any service bond or training-cost clause.
  2. Resign in writing and keep proof. Email to your manager and HR creates a timestamp. Your notice period runs from the date the resignation is given or accepted, depending on your contract.
  3. Get acceptance and the last working day in writing. According to the Nishith Desai note, Indian courts generally hold that an employee cannot withdraw a resignation once the employer has accepted it, and in Air India Express v Gurdarshan Kaur Sandhu the Supreme Court said a prospective resignation can normally be withdrawn before it takes effect unless the contract or rules bar it or the employer has already arranged a replacement.
  4. Ask about early release or buyout early. Do this before you sign a joining date with the new employer.

Early release and notice buyout

An employer may waive all or part of your notice when you ask to leave early, or agree to a shorter period, and it may write into the contract that it can accept payment in lieu of notice (Nishith Desai Associates). The same note says that, beyond payment in lieu, there are no legal provisions on buying out a notice period. In practice that makes buyout a negotiation, not an entitlement.

If you leave without serving notice and without agreement, your employer has a contractual claim against you. The note says labour courts rarely award more than the pay for the unserved notice period unless the employer proves actual losses, and some state laws cap the employee's liability at pro rata salary for that period.

The arithmetic is usually days not served multiplied by a daily rate based on basic or gross pay, depending on your contract. Our notice period buyout calculator works out the figure from your own numbers, including leave set-off. If your new employer is reimbursing the amount, ask whether it is grossed up for tax, because a reimbursement is generally taxed as salary.

Garden leave: paid, but out of the building

Garden leave means you stay on the payroll for some or all of your notice period but are told not to work, contact clients or access systems. Indian labour law does not define it, but employers use it to keep a departing employee away from customers and confidential plans, especially when the person is joining a competitor (Nishith Desai Associates).

Three points matter if you are put on garden leave:

  • You must be paid in full. The note says the employer must continue regular salary and benefits, because the employment relationship continues.
  • It ends when employment ends. In VFS Global v Suprit Roy (2008), the Bombay High Court held that garden leave can be enforced only during employment, not after the termination date. Post-termination non-compete clauses are generally void under Indian contract law.
  • You are still employed. The note says there is no legal bar on dual employment, but full-time employees are generally expected not to work for another employer during the notice period, and contracts usually say so. Do not start the new job until your last working day.

Relieving letters, experience letters and service certificates

New employers often ask for a relieving letter, but the legal position is narrower than many employees assume.

The service certificate

For workers covered by the Model Standing Orders, 2026, the services-sector schedule says every worker is entitled to a service certificate stating the nature of work, designation and period of employment, issued within ten days of discharge, termination, retirement or resignation (Model Standing Orders, 2026). It is a factual record of service, which is what most people mean by an experience letter.

The relieving letter

A relieving letter confirms that you resigned and were released. On 25 June 2026, SCC Online reported a Bombay High Court ruling in a case involving an aircraft maintenance engineer who had signed a three-year service bond after training, resigned early without serving 60 days' notice or paying the ₹10 lakh in liquidated damages the bond set, and then sought a relieving letter and service certificate. The court set aside an Industrial Court order directing the employer to issue them, saying a relieving letter follows a validly accepted resignation, and where refusing to accept the resignation is justified by a breach of contract, the employer cannot be compelled to issue it. The main complaint was sent back for quick adjudication.

Courts have also protected employees. In a 2024 Delhi High Court case summarised by King Stubb & Kasiva, a public-sector employer revoked a senior hire's joining because his previous employer had been slow to process his resignation. The court found he had in fact been relieved and ordered that he be allowed to join within a week with consequential benefits.

The practical lesson: serve or settle your notice cleanly, get acceptance in writing, and clear any bond before you leave. If an employer refuses documents without a contractual basis, a written request followed by a complaint to the labour authorities is the usual route.

Full and final settlement: what you are owed and when

Your full and final settlement, often called "F&F", typically includes salary up to the last working day, encashment of eligible leave, pending reimbursements and bonuses due under your contract, minus any agreed recoveries such as notice shortfall. Gratuity and provident fund are handled separately.

ItemRuleSource
Wages due on resignationWithin two working days of the resignationCode on Wages, 2019, s.17(2)
Dues on termination (standing orders)Before the end of the second working dayModel Standing Orders, 2026, services schedule
Service certificateWithin ten days of exitModel Standing Orders, 2026, services schedule
GratuityAfter five years' continuous service on resignation; one year for fixed-term employeesCode on Social Security, 2020, s.53; PIB

The two-day wage rule is the one most often ignored. Section 17(2) of the Code on Wages says that where an employee has been removed, dismissed or retrenched, or has resigned, the wages payable shall be paid within two working days of the event, though the appropriate government may set a different time limit (Code on Wages, 2019, Indian Kanoon). Many companies still run F&F on a 30 to 60 day cycle by policy. If yours does, ask HR in writing for the wage component on time and the variable items later.

Gratuity is payable on resignation after at least five years of continuous service under section 53 of the Code on Social Security (Indian Kanoon). Fixed-term employees now qualify after one year (PIB). To check how F&F deductions change your take-home, use the in-hand salary calculator on your final month's figures.

Bottom line

Your notice period is mostly a contractual promise, but it is not unlimited: state law, fairness and the courts cap what an employer can demand, and the Labour Codes now put hard deadlines on what the employer owes you at exit. Read your contract before you resign, negotiate early release in writing, and keep records. If you are moving to a new role, our jobs board lists openings from official company career pages.

FAQ

Is a 90-day notice period legal in India?

Yes, a contract can set it, but it must be reasonable, and a state law may set a shorter statutory period for employees. Courts are wary of one-sided terms where the employer's notice is much shorter than yours.

Can my employer refuse to accept my resignation?

It can hold you to your contractual notice period. Refusing acceptance outright is harder to justify, though the Bombay High Court in June 2026 accepted it where an employee had breached a service bond.

Can I join a new company during garden leave?

Not safely. You remain employed until your last working day, and most contracts bar working for anyone else in that time.

How soon must my final salary be paid?

Under section 17(2) of the Code on Wages, wages due to an employee who resigns must be paid within two working days, unless the government has set another limit.

Is an experience letter mandatory?

For workers covered by the Model Standing Orders, 2026, a service certificate showing your role and period of employment must be issued within ten days of exit. For managers outside standing orders, it depends on your contract and company policy.
